records.name: Kebbi
records.current_summary: Kebbi applies Sharia criminal law as part of the twelve-state northern bloc. The parallel Sharia courts hold criminal jurisdiction over Muslim defendants and criminalise same-sex conduct beyond the federal SSMPA, including acts between women. No trans-specific incident, Hisbah activity, or USCIRF case data exists for Kebbi in this dossier. The framework's presence and operational status since 2002 is the finding.  Score 0.024 below the national 0.08. Identical to the other generic-Sharia states in the bloc (Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Katsina, Niger). The enacted capital-capable criminal jurisdiction adds real risk for a Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor facing arrest under a Sharia court rather than a secular magistrate. Above the documented-Hisbah states: Yobe (0.04), Zamfara (0.05).

sources.claim: HRW 2004 report, chapter IV 'The extension of Shari'a to criminal law': Zamfara first re-adopted criminal Shari'a (Shari'a Establishment Law enacted 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000); by 2002 twelve northern states - Kebbi among them - had Shari'a criminal legislation and Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, the only states with such jurisdiction.
NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (403); the underlying source is USCIRF's study of Sharia criminal-law implementation in Kano, Sokoto and Zamfara (173 cases from 2017).

flags: criminalise same-sex conduct beyond the federal SSMPA, including acts between women

freshness.fact: No repeal in Kebbi since the 2019 mapping; Sharia criminal provisions plus the 2014 SSMPA remain in force.

records.name: Niger
records.current_summary: Niger State operates Sharia criminal law within the twelve-state northern bloc adopted by 2002. Sharia courts have jurisdiction over criminal matters for Muslims and the penal code extends criminalisation to same-sex acts between women. No trans-specific incident or documented Hisbah enforcement appears for Niger State in this dossier. The legal architecture adds a parallel criminal-jurisdiction layer absent in the southern secular states.  Score 0.024 below the national 0.08, in the generic-Sharia tier (Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Katsina, Kebbi). The deviation is the enacted system itself; the absence of case-level or enforcement documentation (unlike Kano, Sokoto, Zamfara in the USCIRF study) prevents a deeper cut. Above FCT (0.05), which has a specific trans-person killing and state-implicated failure to investigate despite lacking any Sharia jurisdiction.

sources.claim: HRW 2004 report, chapter IV 'The extension of Shari'a to criminal law': Zamfara first re-adopted criminal Shari'a (Shari'a Establishment Law enacted 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000); by 2002 twelve northern states - Niger State among them - had Shari'a criminal legislation and Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, the only states with such jurisdiction.

UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note, 'Nigeria: Sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics' (version 4.0, June 2025): documents the hybrid legal system and the 12-state Sharia criminal layer, its coverage of women, and arrest-data limits. (Cache captured the front-matter only; content as catalogued in the research dossier.)

flags: the penal code extends criminalisation to same-sex acts between women

freshness.fact: Current source (Jun 2025): Niger State criminalisation unchanged under Sharia provisions applied since 1999-2000 plus the 2014 SSMPA.

records.name: Imo
records.current_summary: Imo State combines mob 'community justice' with active secular SSMPA policing. In April 2018, two men were stripped naked, beaten, and paraded through the streets in Isiala Mbano by a crowd accusing them of gay sex. In February 2025, the Imo State Police Command announced it had 'foiled a same-sex party' at the Graziella Hotel, Owerri West, arresting multiple gay and lesbian suspects, and explicitly named the 14-year SSMPA penalty. The pattern across years and modality (mob then state) supports a regional finding rather than isolated stories.  Score 0.024 below the national 0.08. The 2025 police operation is direct state enforcement naming the criminal law; the 2018 parade is community violence met without accountability. Together they push slightly below the national aggregate, which already absorbs hundreds of such incidents. Above Yobe (0.04) and Zamfara (0.05), which carry the far harsher Sharia capital-punishment framework. On par with Edo (0.06), whose 2018 lynching is comparably severe but lacks Imo's 2025 state-command announcement.

sources.claim: 76crimes report (26 April 2018): two men in Imo State were stripped naked, beaten and paraded through the streets of Isiala Mbano with palm leaves tied round them after being accused of gay sex, by a crowd that filmed and shouted at them; a third man escaped, and a follow-up inquiry reported the two were taken by police. The outlet situates the attack in a rising pattern of mob justice enabled by the 2014 anti-gay law.

Nigerian Newspoint report (19 February 2025): the Imo State Police Command announced it had stormed a 'same-sex party' at the Graziella Hotel, Orogwe, Owerri West LGA on 15 February 2025 after a hotel tip-off, arresting eight named suspects (four women, four men) and charging them under the anti-gay law the command cited as carrying a 14-year term; the command's briefing expressly framed enforcement against 'gay, lesbian, bisexual and/or transgender act', with fleeers still being sought.

flags: Score 0.024 below the national 0.08

records.name: Edo
records.current_summary: In May 2018 in Ekpoma, Edo State, two men were discovered by their community; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. Coverage framed the killing around the local concept of an 'abominable act' defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land' — customary authority operating as a moral-jurisdiction mechanism outside the Sharia belt. No prosecution or accountability is recorded for the killing. The dossier groups Edo with Imo as the 'non-Sharia southeast/west belt' where violent community justice substitutes for formal enforcement.  Score 0.024 below the national 0.08. The lynching is the most lethal single incident outside the Sharia block and the FCT, met with full impunity, qualifying under the 'state-implicated by omission' exception. On par with Imo (0.06), which pairs mob violence with a 2025 state-police operation; Edo's violence is more severe (death) but lacks a comparable recent state-enforcement event. Above the generic Sharia states (0.06, tied) by legal severity: Edo has no capital-punishment statute, but has demonstrated that extralegal lethal violence occurs with zero consequence.

sources.claim: Nigerian Observer news report (May 2018): in Ekpoma, Edo State, two men in their late twenties were discovered having sex by their community; one was lynched to death and the other escaped, in coverage framed around the local concept of an 'abominable act' defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land'. (Cache captured mostly page navigation; incident detail per the research dossier.) No prosecution is recorded for the killing.

The Initiative for Equal Rights (TIERs) '2024 Human Rights Violations Report' (published January 2025): annual documentation of violations based on real or perceived SOGIESC in Nigeria; per the dossier, its 2024 edition records 556 violations affecting 850 victims across the reporting period and states these represent only a fraction of the true scale.

Score 0.024 below the national 0.08

records.name: Aceh
records.current_summary: Aceh operates under a separate Sharia criminal code (Qanun No. 6/2014) that criminalises same-sex conduct as liwath and musahaqah with penalties of up to 100 lashes or eight years' imprisonment—none of which exists in any other Indonesian province. Enforcement by Wilayatul Hisbah Sharia police and Satpol PP is active and escalating: in February 2025 two men caught in a boarding house received a combined 159 lashes publicly in Banda Aceh for consensual sex (one collapsed at the end), and in August 2025 two men received 80 lashes each for hugging and kissing, with the net widening beyond sex to non-sexual contact. A boarding-house raid in February 2025 specifically detained a waria (transfeminine person) alongside a gay student, and in January 2018 police detained and forcibly shaved twelve transwomen.  Deviation from the national score (0.15) is −0.12, the largest single-province gap on this map. A visitor with no criminal conduct elsewhere in Indonesia can be caned in Aceh for the same private behaviour. The Qanun does not name waria explicitly, but the Feb 2025 raid shows enforcement reaches them. No other unit in this country carries an active corporal-punishment regime for consensual adult conduct.  This sits well below West Java (0.08), where the threat is vigilante mob violence with police inaction rather than a codified sentencing framework. Aceh's risk is state-imposed and judicially formalised: Islamic Shariah District Courts hand down caning sentences publicly, sometimes behind closed doors, and the punishment is carried out on a stage in a city park before crowds.

sources.claim: QURU' Journal of Family Law and Culture study (2025), 'The Increasing Number of Waria in Banda Aceh: Between Social Challenges and Law Enforcement': empirical-legal study of how Qanun No. 6 of 2014 on jinayat (liwath, musahaqah, khalwat) is enforced against waria, confirming that Aceh's special Sharia authority includes caning (uqubat cambuk) applied where a violation occurs and that enforcement pressure falls on visible gender nonconformity.

CBS News/AP report (26 Aug 2025): two men aged 20 and 21 were publicly caned 80 strokes each in Banda Aceh's Bustanussalatin park after an Islamic Shariah court convicted them of hugging and kissing (ruled as leading to banned sexual relations), before ~100 spectators, with eight more people caned the same day; notes Aceh permits up to 100 lashes for morality offences (gay sex, unmarried sex, gambling, drinking, women's 'tight' clothing) and that the trial itself was held behind closed doors; Amnesty called it 'state-sanctioned discrimination and cruelty'.

Portal Aceh/iNews report (18 Feb 2025): Banda Aceh Satpol PP and Wilayatul Hisbah detained a pair — a waria and a gay university student — in a boarding-house room; the enforcement unit's Sharia-law enforcement division head confirmed they face up to 100 caning strokes under the Qanun liwath provision and urged kos-house owners to police tenants, showing boarding-house round-ups on this basis are recurring and that waria are swept up in liwath enforcement.

Australian Human Rights Institute (UNSW) commentary: transgender women are the most frequent victims of police violence in Indonesia's anti-LGBT upturn; records the January 2018 case where Aceh police detained twelve transwomen and forcibly shaved/cut their hair to teach them 'how to act like real men', within a national pattern of state failure to protect trans citizens.

records.name: KwaZulu-Natal
records.current_summary: KwaZulu-Natal is the province with both the strongest customary-leadership authority and the most directly documented township queerphobia in South Africa. A criminological field study of KwaMashu township (north of Durban) examines "queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities", situating it within endemic-violence patterns - evidence that the constitutional guarantee does not reach daily life in KZN townships. Additionally, Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini made public anti-gay statements at a 2012 harvest-festival speech, and when a Pietermaritzburg LGBT+ network sought an apology, CONTRALESA (Congress of Traditional Leaders of South Africa) defended the king and condemned "the gays" for seeking fame - royal and chiefly authority aligning against queer people in this specific province.  KZN also sits in the former-Bantustan geography where traditional courts adjudicate morality-adjacent matters under customary law with a consent presumption running against the individual (HRW analysis of the Traditional Courts Bill; the successor Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act 3 of 2019 was declared constitutionally invalid on 30 May 2023 in Mogale and Others, with the declaration suspended and the Act's validity extended to give Parliament time to legislate a replacement). No province has religious criminal law, and no trans-specific arrest or court-blocked statute applies to a visitor here.  The score is 0.06 below the national 0.69. vs. Limpopo (0.65) and North West (0.65), KZN deviates further because it combines the customary-authority jurisdiction with an actual documented field study of queerphobic violence AND the king/CONTRALESA episode; Limpopo and North West carry only the jurisdictional risk without a retrieved provincial trans-incident series. vs. Western Cape (0.72), the gap reflects the presence of a functioning metro NGO/state-institution belt in the Cape versus the township-and-chief authority environment in KZN. The dossier's under-reporting caveat means the absence of a provincial trans-specific incident register here is not exculpatory.

sources.claim: University of KwaZulu-Natal, Criminology and Forensic Studies MA thesis (Buthelezi, 2024): 'A criminological exploration of queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in KwaMashu Township' - documents violence against queer people in a Durban-area township despite the Constitution's equality guarantee, situating it within South Africa's pervasive crime and hate-crime context.

Pink News report (26 January 2012) on the fallout from Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini's anti-gay remarks at a harvest ceremony: the royal family called the reported 'rotten' wording a mistranslation, the South African Human Rights Commission said it would investigate, the KwaZulu-Natal premier backed the royal family, and CONTRALESA said the Pietermaritzburg gay and lesbian network that demanded an apology had shown the king 'disrespect' and were 'only seeking fame'.

records.name: Mpumalanga
records.current_summary: Mpumalanga is geographically attributable as the institutional home of the National House of Traditional Leaders' (NHTL) formal campaign against constitutional equality for queer people. The NHTL—South Africa's official body of tribal chiefs—met at Hazyview, Mpumalanga, and resolved that "traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts," and separately asked Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Daily Maverick commentary identifies this NHTL lobbying, together with the chair of the Constitutional Review Committee, as precisely the mechanism that "intensifies prejudice and hatred" and fuels homophobic violence—an identified official-climate pathway, not merely a statement.  The dossier notes this evidence dates from 2010–2016 and should be treated as durable climate rather than current enacted policy. No provincial statute, no enforcement against a visitor, and no trans-specific incident series is documented. Mpumalanga is not listed in the former-Bantustan traditional-court geography; its risk signal is the formal institutional position taken on its soil, not a parallel legal system operating on visitors. South Africa's Constitution, PEPUDA, and the Hate Crime framework remain uniform and protective at the national level.  The score is 0.04 below the national 0.69. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), Mpumalanga sits higher because KZN adds both a retrieved township queerphobia study and the Zulu king / CONTRALESA episode with an ongoing traditional-court jurisdiction question; Mpumalanga's finding is one resolution and its subsequent lobbying, geographically located but not jurisdictionally operationalised against visitors. vs. Western Cape (0.72), the gap is driven by the absence of a metro NGO belt and the NHTL's public rejection of the equality clause versus the Cape's institutional visibility. vs. Gauteng (0.71), Mpumalanga lacks the representative hate-crime research infrastructure that signals an active civil-society response environment.

sources.claim: Published letter (June 2010) from the NHTL and its Provincial Houses after meeting at Hazyview, Mpumalanga: while 'respecting' the Constitutional Court same-sex marriage judgment, 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts'; states they do not support legalisation of same-sex marriages, warns of ostracism and violence, and vows a five-year campaign against it.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (missing from cache); the underlying 2016 report documents the NHTL asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

records.name: Limpopo
records.current_summary: Limpopo has the highest density of functioning traditional authority in South Africa, making the parallel customary-law jurisdiction most consequential here. HRW's analysis of the traditional-courts legislation (enacted as the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act 3 of 2019) is explicit that it "establishes a separate legal system for people living in the former Bantustans" and "threatens to undermine this security for millions of South Africans living in rural areas," "particularly for the exercise of gender and sexual rights," because chiefs and traditional courts adjudicate personal-status and morality-adjacent matters under customary law with a consent presumption running against the individual. The Act was declared constitutionally invalid in Mogale (ConCourt, 30 May 2023) but validity suspended and extended two years for Parliament to pass a replacement (TKLB, delayed 2023 and 2025).  No provincial trans-specific incident series was retrievable in English sources; this is a jurisdictional finding, not an incident finding. No statute criminalises a visitor's expression, no arrests are documented, and no religious criminal law operates here. The risk to a discovered/outed visitor is that in a rural Limpopo context the local moral authority is a chief's court, not a metro court with an LGBTQ+-trained prosecutor—and the customary-law adjudication of gender/sexuality has historically run against the individual.  The score is 0.04 below the national 0.69. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), Limpopo sits higher because KZN pairs the jurisdictional risk with a retrieved field study of township queerphobic violence AND the Zulu king / CONTRALESA episode; Limpopo's finding is purely the density of the parallel system without a documented trans incident. vs. North West (0.65), the two are comparable: both are former-Bantustan jurisdictions where traditional courts bite, but North West also has a 2010 provincial hate-crime study giving it a data-presence signal. vs. Western Cape (0.72), the gap is metro-institution vs. customary-authority geography. The dossier's under-reporting caveat means the absence of incidents here is not confirmation of safety.

records.name: Gauteng
records.current_summary: Gauteng—where Johannesburg and Pretoria sit—is the best-documented and best-resourced province for an outed trans visitor. It hosts the country's first representative quantitative hate-crime study (OUT LGBT Well-being for the Joint Working Group, 2003/04, 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng'), establishing prevalence, consequences, and contributing factors and signalling an active civil-society and research environment that can respond to incidents. GALA's companion review confirms that only three such studies have ever been done nationally (Gauteng, KZN, Western Cape 2003; North West 2010), placing Gauteng in the tier where evidence, reporting infrastructure, and NGO visibility exist. The HSRC/Global Pride Study analysis names the provincial paradox directly: internationally recognised legal protections coexist with "pervasive violence and discrimination" driven by "gender identity, visibility and health status," meaning Gauteng's courts and NGOs operate alongside genuine risk—but the operating courts and NGOs are the variable that matters for a visitor who is discovered.  For a foreign visitor, the practical difference is institutional: in Gauteng's metro belt, an incident is more likely to be handled by a police station with access to PEPUDA-trained prosecutors and LGBT-aware NGOs than by a chief's court or a township crowd. No province-specific ban, statute, or enforcement action exists. South Africa's constitutional protections (enumeration of sexual orientation and gender identity, PEPUDA, Hate Crime framework) apply uniformly; Gauteng's contribution is that the enforcement machinery behind them is most visible and accessible here. The under-reporting caveat cuts both ways: a province with more recorded hate crime is likelier to have better reporting than more danger.  The score is 0.02 above the national 0.69. vs. Western Cape (0.72), Gauteng sits marginally lower because the Western Cape (Cape Town) has the highest public visibility and the strongest NGO infrastructure per capita, while Gauteng's violence volume—acknowledged in the HSRC analysis—is higher. vs. Limpopo (0.65) and KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), the gap of 0.06–0.08 reflects metro-institutional functioning (courts, prosecutors, reporting) versus the township-and-rural customary-authority environment where the state's response is mediated by a chief's moral adjudication. vs. Northern Cape (0.64), the gap reflects the presence of a 20-year reporting and NGO infrastructure against a province with a recorded trans killing but no comparable civil-society research and reporting infrastructure.

sources.claim: 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors' - Joint Working Group research initiative conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being with the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology (authors Wells & Polders), the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa (2003/04); partner roster includes Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016): the companion review of hate crimes against LGBT people in South Africa states that only three quantitative studies have ever been done - the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape; a 2010 North West province study; and this national campaign study - and measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

records.name: Chechnya
records.current_summary: Chechnya operates outside the Russian federal legal framework in practice. In February 2017, Chechen law-enforcement and security officials launched an anti-gay purge, rounding up dozens of men, holding them in unofficial detention facilities (documented by name and location, including a secret prison in Argun), humiliating, starving, and torturing them, forcibly disappearing some, and returning others to families "barely alive from beatings" after captors exposed them and encouraged relatives to carry out honour killings (HRW, 2017). Novaya Gazeta reported in January 2019 that persecution had resumed and the Argun facility was "full again," while Kadyrov's press chief publicly denied any unofficial detention sites exist.  The pattern has mutated and continues: North Caucasus SOS documented at least seven cases of Chechen security forces blackmailing detained homosexual men into "volunteering" for front-line conscription in Ukraine (one already killed), and Memorial found a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced conscription. In 2021, Kadyrov's aide announced the abduction of two men evacuated abroad, taken at the Gudermes police station. The UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) explicitly names the North Caucasus as the exception to its finding of no state-persecution risk elsewhere in Russia.  For a visitor discovered or outed, the evidence indicates near-certain detention without legal process, torture, coerced conscription or death, with no functioning judicial remedy. This is approximately 0.11 below the national score of 0.12, reflecting a governance system where the state's security apparatus operates outside all legal constraint. Far below every other unit in the federation; even Dagestan and Ingushetia (0.04), which share the North Caucasus security logic, lack Chechnya's documented scale of extrajudicial killing and secret-prison infrastructure.
